articles.title: The Slow Death of the Monolith Myth
articles.dek: A decade of microservice enthusiasm produced fewer resilient systems than its advocates promised — and a great deal more network.
body: The argument for splitting an application into services was never really about the services. It was about teams: the promise that an organisation could scale its headcount without every change requiring every engineer's agreement. That promise was real, and for a handful of companies operating at genuinely enormous scale it paid for itself many times over.

What travelled less well was the assumption underneath it. A function call that cannot fail became a network call that can, and the failure modes multiplied faster than the tooling to observe them. The industry spent ten years rebuilding, in YAML and sidecars, guarantees the compiler used to provide for free.
articles.author: dilek-arslan

articles.title: What a Cache Key Actually Costs
articles.dek: Every discriminator you add to a cache key is a hit rate you give away. Most systems choose badly, and quietly.
body: Caching looks like a storage problem and behaves like a taxonomy problem. The hard question is never how many entries fit in memory; it is which requests should be considered the same request. Get that wrong in one direction and you serve one reader another reader's page. Get it wrong in the other and your cache holds a thousand copies of an identical article, one per tracking parameter.

The honest default is to include everything the response could possibly depend on and accept the fragmentation. The optimisation — an allowlist of the parameters that actually change the output — is straightforward to build and impossible to get right generically, because only the application knows which of its query parameters are decoration.
articles.author: dilek-arslan

articles.title: The Index That Ate the Database
articles.dek: A single well-meaning index turned a four-millisecond query into a twenty-minute outage. The postmortem is a lesson in humility.
body: The change was two lines and reviewed by three people. It added an index on a column that appeared in a slow query, which is the most ordinary thing a backend engineer does in a given week. It shipped on a Tuesday afternoon and the alerts started ninety minutes later.

What nobody had modelled was the write path. The table took eleven thousand inserts a second at peak, and every one of them now had a second B-tree to maintain. The reads got faster exactly as predicted; the writes fell off a cliff, the replication lag grew without bound, and the read replicas that were supposed to absorb the load began serving data forty minutes stale.
articles.author: tomas-lindqvist

articles.title: Nobody Reads the Error Message
articles.dek: Interface designers have spent thirty years making failures quieter. The result is systems that fail invisibly and users who have learned not to look.
body: There is a design lineage that runs from the modal dialog box to the small grey toast that fades after four seconds, and it is a lineage of retreat. Each step made errors less intrusive, which was framed as respect for the user's attention. In practice it taught people that an error is something you wait out rather than something you read.

The cost lands on support teams, who now field reports in the form of a shrug. The screenshot arrives with the notification already gone. The state that caused it is unrecoverable. The engineer asks what the message said and is told, accurately, that it was grey.
articles.author: dilek-arslan

articles.title: The Protein Fold That Would Not Cooperate
articles.dek: Prediction models solved a fifty-year problem. A small, stubborn class of structures is still defeating them, and the reasons are interesting.
body: The structure prediction results that arrived at the start of the decade were not incremental. A problem that had consumed careers became, for most proteins, a question you could answer in an afternoon on a laptop. The field's response was appropriately dramatic, and appropriately short-lived: within two years the interesting work had moved to the residue.

Intrinsically disordered regions do not have a structure to predict. They adopt different conformations depending on what they are bound to, which means the question the model was trained to answer is not well posed for them. They are also, by some counts, present in a third of human proteins and enriched precisely in the signalling pathways that matter for disease.
articles.author: marcus-obi

articles.title: Replication Is Not a Scandal
articles.dek: The replication crisis was reported as a failure of science. It was closer to the opposite, and treating it otherwise has done real damage.
body: When large replication projects began reporting that half of the studies they retested did not hold up, the coverage wrote itself. The finding was framed as an indictment, and in the years since, it has been cited approvingly by people with no interest in improving research methods and considerable interest in ignoring research conclusions.

The framing was wrong in a specific way. A field that discovers its own error rate, publishes it, and changes its practices is a field in working order. The alarming condition would have been never checking. What the projects actually exposed was a publication system that rewarded novelty over reliability — an incentive problem, fixable and being fixed, not an epistemological collapse.
articles.author: marcus-obi

articles.title: The Telescope That Sees Too Much
articles.dek: Modern surveys produce more candidate events than any group of astronomers can examine. Deciding what to ignore is now the science.
body: A wide-field survey instrument can flag several million transient candidates a night. Almost all of them are artefacts: cosmic ray hits, satellite trails, the subtraction residue left when a bright star is imperfectly removed from a reference frame. The genuine astrophysical events are a rounding error inside the noise.

This has quietly inverted the discipline. The rare skill is no longer the observation; it is the classifier, and the judgement encoded in its training set about what counts as uninteresting. Every survey therefore has a blind spot shaped exactly like the phenomena nobody thought to label.
articles.author: marcus-obi

articles.title: Archives Are a Budget Line
articles.dek: What a culture preserves is decided less by historians than by whoever signs off on storage renewals.
body: Preservation is discussed as though it were a scholarly judgement and practised as though it were a procurement decision, because it is. A national collection's holdings reflect a century of acquisitions, but what remains accessible reflects last year's operating budget and the particular formats that happened to be cheap to migrate.

The losses are rarely dramatic. Nobody burns anything. A format falls out of support, the one working playback device fails, the specialist who knew the catalogue retires, and the material becomes technically extant and practically gone. It stays on the inventory, which is how the loss escapes notice for another decade.
articles.author: helena-strand

articles.title: The Museum That Gave It Back
articles.dek: A restitution that took eleven years, and what the delay reveals about how institutions actually decide.
body: The claim was filed in 2015 and the objects went home this spring. Between those dates sat no serious dispute about provenance — the acquisition record was unusually clear, and the institution's own researchers had said so in writing by 2017. What sat there instead was process.

Eleven years is not how long it takes to establish a fact. It is how long it takes an organisation to accept a conclusion its structure was not built to reach, through committees that could defer but not decide, under trustees whose duty of care was written for a world in which holding on was always the safe option.
articles.author: helena-strand

articles.title: Nostalgia Is a Distribution Strategy
articles.dek: The revival cycle has compressed to about eight years. That is not a cultural shift; it is a licensing calculation.
body: There is a comfortable story in which each generation rediscovers the aesthetics of its childhood, and the roughly twenty-year revival cycle follows from human development. It is a good story and the timing no longer fits it. The gap has been closing for two decades and is now shorter than the childhood it supposedly recalls.

The better explanation is duller and better documented. Catalogue rights are a known quantity with a known audience and no marketing risk, which makes them the safest thing a platform can commission against. Revivals arrive when the licensing window opens, and the windows have been getting shorter.
articles.author: helena-strand

articles.title: The Forecast Nobody Wanted
articles.dek: Analysts were broadly right about the downturn and broadly ignored. The failure was not prediction; it was incentive.
body: Going back through the published research from eighteen months before the correction, the striking thing is not that the warnings were absent. They were there, in the risk sections, hedged but legible, from most of the major desks. What was absent was any consequence for ignoring them.

A sell-side analyst who calls a downturn early is wrong for several quarters before being right for one. The career mathematics are unambiguous and everyone involved can do the arithmetic. The result is a body of research that contains the correct answer in a subordinate clause and the comfortable answer in the headline.
articles.author: ravi-chandrasekhar

articles.title: Why Your Company Cannot Say No
articles.dek: Organisations accumulate commitments with no mechanism for shedding them. The consequences take about five years to show up.
body: Every large organisation has a process for starting things. Very few have a process for stopping them, and the asymmetry compounds. A project that no longer serves any purpose requires someone to say so, in public, about work that colleagues did in good faith, with no reward attached to being the one who says it.

So the portfolio grows. Maintenance obligations accrete against a headcount that was sized for the original scope. Nothing fails visibly; the organisation simply becomes slower, and the slowness is attributed to size rather than to the decade of undeclared commitments underneath it.
articles.author: ravi-chandrasekhar

articles.title: The Productivity Number Is Lying
articles.dek: Output per hour is measured with tools designed for factories and applied to work that produces nothing you can count.
body: The measure was built when the representative worker made things. Divide units produced by hours worked and you have a number that means something, tracks something real, and improves when the process improves. It was a good instrument for the economy it was designed against.

Applied to an economy in which most people produce decisions, coordination and care, it reports mostly noise. A nurse who spends longer with a patient registers as less productive. A team that prevents an outage produces nothing measurable at all. The statistic has not stopped being computed, or cited in policy, on account of this.
articles.author: tomas-lindqvist

articles.title: Seawalls Buy Time, Not Safety
articles.dek: Coastal defences work, which is exactly why they are dangerous: they make the protected land worth developing.
body: The engineering is not in doubt. A properly specified barrier will hold back the design storm and has done so repeatedly. The difficulty is what happens on the dry side of it over the following thirty years, which is that the land stops being treated as exposed.

Development follows protection. Property values rise, density increases, and the population behind the wall grows past what the design assumed, while the design storm itself grows too. The wall does not fail more often; it fails worse. Planners have a name for it and no consistent answer to it.
articles.author: noor-haddad

articles.title: The Heat Ordinance That Worked
articles.dek: A municipal rule with no climate language in it cut heat deaths by a third. Its authors would rather you did not call it climate policy.
body: The ordinance requires a maximum indoor temperature in rented housing, mandates cooling in common areas of buildings above a certain size, and obliges landlords to repair a failed system within seventy-two hours. It reads as a housing regulation because it is one, and it passed a council that had rejected two climate resolutions in the preceding year.

Three summers of mortality data now sit behind it, and the effect is large and concentrated exactly where the modelling said it would be: elderly tenants in older buildings on upper floors. The lesson its drafters draw is not about heat. It is that the framing which passes is the framing that survives the committee.
articles.author: noor-haddad

articles.title: Carbon Accounting Is Mostly Accounting
articles.dek: Corporate emissions disclosures have become a genre of financial reporting, with all the discretion that implies.
body: Scope three — the emissions a company causes but does not directly produce — is where the interesting choices live. It is also, for most firms, the overwhelming majority of the total, which means the headline figure is largely a function of boundary decisions made by the firm reporting it.

None of this requires anyone to lie. Every judgement can be defensible in isolation: this supplier is out of scope, that estimate uses an industry average, this category is immaterial. Aggregate enough defensible judgements in one direction and you have a number that is both fully compliant and not usefully comparable to any other company's.
articles.author: noor-haddad

articles.title: The Grid Is the Hard Part
articles.dek: Generation got cheap faster than anyone forecast. Transmission did not, and that is now the binding constraint.
body: The cost curves for solar and wind generation outran every serious projection made in the preceding decade, including the optimistic ones. That part of the transition is, in economic terms, finished: the cheap option is now also the clean one across most of the world, without subsidy.

Moving the electricity is another matter. A transmission line takes ten to fifteen years from proposal to energisation in most jurisdictions, and almost none of that is construction. It is permitting, land acquisition, and litigation — processes that were designed to slow things down and are performing exactly as designed.
articles.author: noor-haddad

articles.title: The Interview That Never Happened
articles.dek: A profile built entirely from public record, and what it says about access journalism that it reads no differently.
body: The subject declined, twice, through a representative who was polite about it. The resulting piece used court filings, three decades of trade press, two depositions, a planning application and eleven interviews with people who had worked for him. It ran at nine thousand words.

What it did not contain was a single quotation from the man himself, and in the reporting that followed nobody appeared to notice. That is the uncomfortable finding. The access adds atmosphere, a scene in a car, a revealing aside — and in exchange the subject acquires a say in the framing that the record never grants him.
articles.author: tomas-lindqvist

articles.title: Open Source Maintainers Are Not Volunteers
articles.dek: The word flatters everyone involved and describes almost nobody. The funding conversation cannot start until it is dropped.
body: A volunteer chooses the work and can stop. The person maintaining a library that four thousand companies depend on has a pager, a security disclosure queue, and a backlog of issues filed by people who are being paid to file them. The relationship has every structural feature of employment except compensation and the ability to resign without consequence.

Calling it volunteering makes the arrangement sound like generosity rather than a transfer, which is convenient for the side receiving it. The maintainers themselves often use the word, which is part of why the funding models that have been tried keep being framed as charity — and why they keep raising roughly what charity raises.
articles.author: tomas-lindqvist

articles.title: The Standard That Shipped Too Early
articles.dek: A specification finalised before anyone had implemented it twice, and the decade of workarounds that followed.
body: Standards bodies have a rule of thumb about requiring two independent interoperating implementations before a specification is declared final. It exists because a document can be internally consistent, unambiguous, and still describe something nobody can build efficiently. The rule was waived here, for scheduling reasons that were entirely understandable at the time.

The first implementation revealed an ambiguity in the state machine that two reasonable readings resolved differently. Both readings shipped. Because the specification was final, neither could be declared wrong, and the resolution was a negotiation extension that every implementation now supports and the specification still does not mention.
articles.author: dilek-arslan
